| [LIT-553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-553.md) | Psychological Flexibility as a Fundamental Aspect of Health | Kashdan & Rottenberg (2010), Clinical Psychology Review 30(7):865–878. Psychological health is not a ratio of positive to negative experience or a set of fixed strengths but flexibility: adapting regulation to the situation, balancing time perspectives and life domains, and acting on values while open to experience. Inflexibility marks depression (rumination, emotion context insensitivity) and anxiety (experiential avoidance), and cardiac vagal control is proposed as an integrating marker. Executive functioning, default states and personality underlie it, and dynamic measurement is needed. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-436](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-436.md)), in the NIH author manuscript on PubMed Central; worth reading as the review that took "psychological flexibility" out of the ACT literature and made it a general construct of health. Flexibility is adapting to situational demands, reconfiguring mental resources, shifting perspective and balancing competing desires and life domains. Its absence (rumination, emotion context insensitivity, experiential avoidance, low cardiac vagal control) runs through depression and anxiety. Executive functioning, default mental states and personality are its "building blocks". It is a narrative synthesis: no meta-analysis of its own, the causal direction between inflexibility and disorder is left open by its own account, and it asks for dynamic measures in place of the global self-reports the ACT line relies on. |
| [LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md) | The "What" and "Why" of Goal Pursuits: Human Needs and the Self-Determination of Behavior | Deci & Ryan (2000), Psychological Inquiry 11(4):227–268, target article. SDT's case for innate psychological needs, for competence, relatedness and autonomy, defined as nutriments for growth, integrity and well-being and identified functionally, against Hull's drives and Murray's acquired needs. The "why" of a goal (autonomous or controlled regulation) and its "what" (intrinsic or extrinsic aspiration) each predict well-being, because each affects need satisfaction. Thwarted needs yield substitutes, controlled styles and rigid patterns. SDT grounds autonomy in the organism's tendency to self-organize, argued to be an evolved advantage. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-439](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-439.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published target article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the full statement of what SDT means by a "need" and why it posits three. Needs are "innate psychological nutriments that are essential for ongoing psychological growth, integrity, and well-being" (p. 228), identified by what follows when they are satisfied or thwarted, not by how strongly people want them. Goals differ in their "why" (autonomous or controlled regulation) and their "what" (intrinsic or extrinsic content), and both matter because of need satisfaction. Thwarting produces need substitutes, controlled regulatory styles and rigid behaviour patterns. It is a target article: the commentaries and the authors' reply in the same issue were not read. |

The article is open access under CC BY: the publisher's PDF at link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11031-019-09800-x.pdf returned a client challenge (bot check) to curl, and the authors' submitted version in Aalto University's repository, research.aalto.fi/files/38294637/Martela_Ryan2019_Article_DistinguishingBetweenBasicPsyc.pdf, returned a Cloudflare "Just a moment" page. Neither host was retried. A web search found no other copy (selfdeterminationtheory.org holds the 2016 beneficence paper, not this one). A browser fetch of either address is the cheapest way to read it. Until then what the record holds of it is second-hand, in NOTE-440. |
| [LIT-1988](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1988.md) v2 | Assessing basic/fundamental psychological need fulfillment: systematic mapping and review of existing scales to foster cumulative science | Kermavnar, Avsec, Huang and Desmet (2024), Frontiers in Psychology 15. A PRISMA review, searched 21 August 2023, of original self-report scales of need fulfillment in healthy general populations: 31 scales from 32 primary studies, 23 based on self-determination theory, with 89 adaptations. 21 measure satisfaction only; four satisfaction and frustration, three support, one frustration only (2020), one thwarting (Bartholomew et al. 2011), one support and thwarting. Autonomy appears in 27 scales, relatedness 24, competence 23, over 30 other needs in a few each. The review documents the four states' terms used interchangeably, double-barrelled frustration-thwarting items, satisfaction items that ask about thwarting, and the BPNSFS's frustration scales "repurposed" from negatively coded satisfaction items (after Murphy et al. 2023). It finds no consensus on what makes a need basic, takes no side on the two-dimensional model, and names the IBQ and GNSF as good practice. | Active — read in full 2026-11-03 ([NOTE-1509](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1509.md)), from the version of record (CC BY) via Europe PMC; worth reading as a finding aid to the 31 original need-fulfillment scales and as a plain list of the field's measurement faults: satisfaction, frustration, support and thwarting confused, frustration scales built from negatively worded satisfaction items, double-barrelled items. It offers no criterion for need-hood ([THEORY-1318](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1318.md)). |
| [LIT-2000](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2000.md) v2 | Basic psychological need satisfaction, need frustration, and need strength across four cultures | Chen et al. (2015), Motiv. Emot. 39, online 12 November 2014. Two cross-sectional studies, Belgium and China (N = 683) and Belgium, China, the USA and Peru (N = 1,051). They build the 24-item Basic Psychological Need Satisfaction and Frustration Scale: six factors fit better than three and are metric-invariant across the four countries. Satisfaction relates mainly to life satisfaction and vitality, frustration mainly to depressive symptoms, with no detectable country differences and no moderation by need valuation or need desire. All frustration items are negatively worded and all satisfaction items positively. | Active — read in full 2026-11-03 ([NOTE-1527](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1527.md)), from the publisher's typeset copy in the ULB repository DI-fusion; worth reading as the source of the BPNSFS, the standard need-frustration scale, and for its test that need satisfaction helps regardless of how much a person values or desires the need. Its satisfaction/frustration split coincides with item direction by construction. |
| [LIT-2152](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2152.md) | On the psychology of poverty | Haushofer & Fehr (2014), a Science Review. Poverty causes stress and negative affect (correlations, and 25 causal studies of which 18 find poverty relief improves well-being or stress, including the first author's Kenya cash-transfer trial); stress and negative affect make people more present-biased and risk-averse (laboratory inductions only). Together these "may constitute a feedback loop that contributes to the perpetuation of poverty". The authors frame this against blame: "we are not suggesting that the poor bear blame for their poverty". They call the affect-to-choice link "the weakest link", find that income and psychological outcomes "show no strong signs of being nonlinear", so the loop is not shown to be a trap, and report no labour-supply or effort responses to transfers. | Active — read in full 2026-11-05 ([NOTE-1681](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1681.md)) from the Science reprint posted on the first author's Stockholm University page, with the supplement's search strategy and factor analysis; worth reading as the standard statement that poverty itself, through stress and negative affect, can produce the short horizons and caution read as the poor's character, and as an explicit case against blaming the poor. Its own limits: a narrative Review with systematic searches, no meta-analysis or pooled effects; the affect-to-choice link, which the authors call "the weakest link", rests on small laboratory inductions only; no nonlinearity strong enough for a poverty trap has been found; persistence after poverty relief is unknown; several key studies are the authors' own. |
